newsitem.title: CHINA: HK-Taipei bridge is strictly business - analysts.
newsitem.headline: HK-Taipei bridge is strictly business - analysts.

text.p: The first contact between Taiwan and Hong Kong's new leader has touched off speculation that the ex-British colony could become a conduit for resolving the Taiwan question.
But analysts say the notion that Hong Kong will play some kind of shuttle diplomacy role between Taipei and Beijing, now that the territory has reverted to China, is far-fetched.

This week's "unofficial" diplomatic exchanges between Hong Kong and Taipei, and Beijing's reaction, confirmed the continuation of a prior, triangular business relationship, and carried no major political implications, analysts said.

"The idea that now Hong Kong is part of China, things will immediately settle down (with Hong Kong assuming) a shuttle diplomacy role between Taiwan and the mainland seems to me to be a little far-fetched," said Richard Margolis, political analyst at Merrill Lynch.
"I think Hong Kong serves best as a bridge between Taiwan and the mainland by concentrating on business," he said.
Taiwan investment in China is estimated at up to US$30 billion, nearly all of which flowed through Hong Kong.

As a British colony, Hong Kong played a lucrative role as a gateway through which two of Asia's most vibrant economies could do business despite a 48-year ban on direct business, transport and communications links.
Direct ties between Taipei and Beijing were axed in 1949, when China's Communists won the civil war on the mainland and the defeated Nationalist government fled to Taiwan.
But the rivals' interest in indirect economic ties throughout China's two-decade-old reform era has overcome the political tension -- much to Hong Kong's benefit.

On Thursday a round of unofficial chat between Hong Kong and Taipei essentially confirmed that the prior, triangular business relationship will continue unchanged despite Hong Kong's return to the motherland's embrace.
"This was a public signal that things would carry on largely as before," Margolis said. "I think the issue has been overplayed."

Both Taipei and Hong Kong's post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa appointed high-level intermediaries to facilitate contact after a round of unofficial talks on the fringes of events connected to Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule.
Domestic newspapers responded with enthusiasm to attempts to lend the exchanges an "official" tone.
But analysts -- and Beijing -- stressed Hong Kong and Taipei retain only an "unofficial" relationship restricted to business.

"(Hong Kong) is to be a stepping-stone to reunification with Taiwan...Hong Kong will be that corner of China where all Chinese people can come together and feel as one," said the Hong Kong Standard in an editorial in tune with Chinese newspapers.
When Beijing designed the "one country, two systems" policy for Hong Kong's return to China, it also had Taiwan in mind.
But Taiwan, which China brands a rebel province, insists national unification can spring only from democracy, freedom and equitable prosperity.
Another analyst said Hong Kong's new status as a part of China signals a fundamental change in its role as anchor for business ties between Beijing and Taipei.
Despite attempts to reassure everyone that things will continue as they have in the past, a new relationship clearly needs to be established.
"It is very difficult to judge at this point the political implications, although the business side will definitely expand," said the analyst.

"Both Taiwan and China are still not quite clear what exact position they should take. They want to wait and see rather than take a firm position. They are testing each other. I don't think a clear picture will emerge for some months."
But Margolis said that so far, strong Taiwan-China economic ties routed through Hong Kong have had little political impact.

"Although I do expect the business relationship to continue to develop because it has a momentum of its own, it's difficult to argue on the basis of past experience that this will necessarily bring a negotiated solution (to the China-Taiwan split) any nearer," Margolis said.
"It may make a solution by military force even less likely than it is now, but whether it would bring a negotiated solution any nearer is a moot point, I would say."
